claim: Cell-to-cell viral infection is a mode in which viruses spread through contact of infected cell with surrounding uninfected cells.
source: Cell-to-cell viral infection, in which viruses spread through contact of infected cell with surrounding uninfected cells, has been considered as a critical mode of virus infection.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract introduction.

claim: It is technically difficult to experimentally discriminate cell-free infection from cell-to-cell infection.
source: However, since it is technically difficult to experimentally discriminate the two modes of viral infection, namely cell-free infection and cell-to-cell infection, the quantitative information that underlies cell-to-cell infection has yet to be elucidated, and its impact on virus spread remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation in current experimental approaches.

claim: Cell-to-cell infection mode accounts for approximately 60% of viral infection.
source: Our analyses demonstrated that the cell-to-cell infection mode accounts for approximately 60% of viral infection, and this infection mode shortens the generation time of viruses by 0.9 times and increases the viral fitness by 3.9 times.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mathematical-experimental analysis presented in the study.

claim: Cell-to-cell infection shortens the generation time of viruses by 0.9 times.
source: Our analyses demonstrated that the cell-to-cell infection mode accounts for approximately 60% of viral infection, and this infection mode shortens the generation time of viruses by 0.9 times and increases the viral fitness by 3.9 times.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the mathematical modeling analysis.

claim: Cell-to-cell infection increases viral fitness by 3.9 times.
source: Our analyses demonstrated that the cell-to-cell infection mode accounts for approximately 60% of viral infection, and this infection mode shortens the generation time of viruses by 0.9 times and increases the viral fitness by 3.9 times.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the mathematical modeling analysis.

claim: A complete block of cell-free infection would provide only a limited impact on HIV-1 spread.
source: Our results suggest that even a complete block of the cell-free infection would provide only a limited impact on HIV-1 spread.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results showing the predominance of cell-to-cell infection.

claim: Both cell-free and cell-to-cell transmission require the assembly of infectious virus particles.
source: Both transmission means require the assembly of infectious virus particles (Monel et al., 2012), which are released in the extracellular medium for cell-free transmission, or concentrated in the confined space of cell-to-cell contacts between an infected cell and bystander target cells in the case of cell-to-cell transmission.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Monel et al., 2012.

claim: Most enveloped virus species, including HIV-1, spread via cell-to-cell infection.
source: It has been shown that most enveloped virus species, including human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1), a causative agent of AIDS, spread via cell-to-cell infection, and it is considered that the replication efficacy of cell-to-cell infection is much higher than that of cell-free infection (Sattentau, 2008; Martin and Sattentau, 2009; Talbert-Slagle et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The replication efficacy of cell-to-cell infection is much higher than that of cell-free infection.
source: It has been shown that most enveloped virus species, including human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1), a causative agent of AIDS, spread via cell-to-cell infection, and it is considered that the replication efficacy of cell-to-cell infection is much higher than that of cell-free infection (Sattentau, 2008; Martin and Sattentau, 2009; Talbert-Slagle et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: It is technically impossible to let viruses execute only cell-to-cell infection.
source: However, it is technically impossible to let viruses execute only cell-to-cell infection.
evidence: This is stated as a technical limitation in experimental virology.

claim: The two infection processes (cell-free and cell-to-cell) occur in a synergistic (nonlinear) manner.
source: In addition, since these two infection processes occur in a synergistic (i.e., nonlinear) manner, the additive (i.e., linear) idea that 'total infection' minus 'cell-free infection' is equal to 'cell-to-cell infection' does not hold true universally.
evidence: This is an inference from the biological understanding of the infection processes.

claim: Different reports provided different estimates of the efficacies of cell-free and cell-to-cell infection.
source: Hence, it was difficult to estimate and compare the efficacies of cell-free and cell-to-cell infection, and different reports provided different estimates (Dimitrov et al., 1993; Carr et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2007; Sourisseau et al., 2007; Zhong et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations showing variability in previous estimates.

claim: The efficacy of cell-to-cell HIV-1 infection is 1.4-fold higher than that of cell-free infection.
source: In this study, through coupled experimental and mathematical investigation, we demonstrate that the efficacy of cell-to-cell HIV-1 infection is 1.4-fold higher than that of cell-free infection (i.e., cell-to-cell infection accounts for approximately 60% of total infection).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental and mathematical analysis.

claim: Cell-to-cell infection increases viral fitness by 3.9 times.
source: We also show that the cell-to-cell infection shortens the generation time of viruses by 0.9 times, and increases the viral fitness by 3.9 times.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the mathematical modeling.

claim: Cell-to-cell infection plays a critical role in efficient and rapid spread of viral infection.
source: These findings strongly suggest that the cell-to-cell infection plays a critical role in efficient and rapid spread of viral infection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the quantitative findings about generation time and viral fitness.

claim: Shaking cell culture prevents cell-to-cell infection by inhibiting cell-to-cell contact formation.
source: On the other hand, Sourisseau et al. have reported that the cell-to-cell infection can be prevented by mildly shaking the cell culture infected with viruses (Sourisseau et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sourisseau et al., 2007.

claim: Shaking does not induce nonspecific consequences on HIV-1 infection.
source: Consistent with the previous report (Sourisseau et al., 2007), we verified that shaking did not induce nonspecific consequences on HIV-1 infection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is verified experimentally and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Static cultures of Jurkat cells allow HIV-1 to propagate both by cell-free and cell-to-cell infection.
source: Static cultures of Jurkat cells, an HIV-1-susceptible human CD4+ T-cell line, allow HIV-1 to propagate both by the cell-free and cell-to-cell infection, while under shaking conditions, Jurkat cells allows HIV-1 to replicate only by the cell-free infection (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is the experimental design described and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Under shaking conditions, Jurkat cells allow HIV-1 to replicate only by cell-free infection.
source: Static cultures of Jurkat cells, an HIV-1-susceptible human CD4+ T-cell line, allow HIV-1 to propagate both by the cell-free and cell-to-cell infection, while under shaking conditions, Jurkat cells allows HIV-1 to replicate only by the cell-free infection (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is the experimental design described and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Previous mathematical models essentially describe only the cell-free infection or implicitly both infection modes.
source: Previous mathematical models, which have been widely used for data analyses, essentially describe only the cell-free infection (Nowak and May, 2000; Perelson, 2002; Iwami et al., 2012a, 2012b) or implicitly both infection modes (Komarova and Wodarz, 2013; Komarova et al., 2013a, 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous modeling work.

claim: The mathematical model (Equations 1-3) describes HIV-1 infection data very well.
source: The typical behavior of the model using these best-fit parameter estimates is shown together with the data in Figure 2, which reveals that Equations 1–3 describe these in vitro data very well.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model fit to experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The basic reproduction number R0 consists of two sub-reproduction numbers: Rcf (cell-free) and Rcc (cell-to-cell).
source: Interestingly, in spite of nonlinear interaction between the two modes of virus transmission, our derivation of R0 revealed that the secondly infected cells were the sum of the basic reproduction number through the cell-free infection Rcf = βpTmax/δc and the basic reproduction number through the cell-to-cell infection Rcc = ωTmax/δ, (i.e., R0 = Rcf + Rcc) (see Figure 1B).
evidence: This is derived mathematically and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The mean total basic reproductive number R0 is 5.83 ± 0.94.
source: Using all accepted MCMC parameter estimates from the time-course experimental datasets, we calculated that on average the mean of the total basic reproductive number is R0 = 5.83 ± 0.94 (average ± standard deviation), and the mean number of secondly infected cells through the cell-free infection and the cell-to-cell infection are Rcf = 2.44 ± 0.23 and Rcc = 3.39 ± 0.91, respectively (see Table 1).
evidence: This is calculated from MCMC parameter estimates and shown in Table 1.

claim: The mean number of secondly infected cells through cell-free infection (Rcf) is 2.44 ± 0.23.
source: Using all accepted MCMC parameter estimates from the time-course experimental datasets, we calculated that on average the mean of the total basic reproductive number is R0 = 5.83 ± 0.94 (average ± standard deviation), and the mean number of secondly infected cells through the cell-free infection and the cell-to-cell infection are Rcf = 2.44 ± 0.23 and Rcc = 3.39 ± 0.91, respectively (see Table 1).
evidence: This is calculated from MCMC parameter estimates and shown in Table 1.

claim: The mean number of secondly infected cells through cell-to-cell infection (Rcc) is 3.39 ± 0.91.
source: Using all accepted MCMC parameter estimates from the time-course experimental datasets, we calculated that on average the mean of the total basic reproductive number is R0 = 5.83 ± 0.94 (average ± standard deviation), and the mean number of secondly infected cells through the cell-free infection and the cell-to-cell infection are Rcf = 2.44 ± 0.23 and Rcc = 3.39 ± 0.91, respectively (see Table 1).
evidence: This is calculated from MCMC parameter estimates and shown in Table 1.

claim: The contribution of cell-to-cell infection is 0.57 ± 0.07 (approximately 60%).
source: These estimates indicate that the contribution of the cell-to-cell infection is almost 60% on average (i.e., Rcc/(Rcc + Rcf) = 0.57 ± 0.07: Table 1) and this mode of infection is predominant during the HIV-1 spread in Jurkat cells.
evidence: This is calculated from the basic reproduction numbers and shown in Table 1.

claim: Cell-to-cell infection is the predominant mode during HIV-1 spread in Jurkat cells.
source: These estimates indicate that the contribution of the cell-to-cell infection is almost 60% on average (i.e., Rcc/(Rcc + Rcf) = 0.57 ± 0.07: Table 1) and this mode of infection is predominant during the HIV-1 spread in Jurkat cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the quantitative analysis showing 60% contribution.

claim: This estimation is consistent with that by Komarova and Wodarz (2013), Komarova et al. (2013a), and Komarova et al. (2013b).
source: Interestingly, this estimation is consistent with that by Komarova and Wodarz (2013), Komarova et al. (2013a), and Komarova et al. (2013b), although they did not take into account the difference of the death rate in the shaking and static conditions.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous modeling studies.

claim: In the presence of cell-to-cell infection, the mean generation time is 2.22 ± 0.32 days.
source: In the presence and absence of the cell-to-cell infection (i.e., for the static and shaking cell cultures, respectively), the mean generation time is calculated as 1/δ + Rcf/cR0 = 2.22 ± 0.32 days and 1/δ + 1/c = 2.47 ± 0.32 days, respectively (see Table 2).
evidence: This is calculated from the mathematical model and shown in Table 2.

claim: In the absence of cell-to-cell infection, the mean generation time is 2.47 ± 0.32 days.
source: In the presence and absence of the cell-to-cell infection (i.e., for the static and shaking cell cultures, respectively), the mean generation time is calculated as 1/δ + Rcf/cR0 = 2.22 ± 0.32 days and 1/δ + 1/c = 2.47 ± 0.32 days, respectively (see Table 2).
evidence: This is calculated from the mathematical model and shown in Table 2.

claim: Cell-to-cell infection shortens the generation time by on average 0.90 times.
source: Thus, cell-to-cell infection shortens the generation time by on average 0.90 times, and enables HIV-1 to efficiently infect target cells (Sato et al., 1992; Carr et al., 1999).
evidence: This is calculated from the generation times with and without cell-to-cell infection.

claim: In the presence of cell-to-cell infection, the Malthus coefficient is 1.86 ± 0.37 per day.
source: In the presence and absence of the cell-to-cell infection, the Malthus coefficient is calculated as 1.86 ± 0.37 and 0.49 ± 0.05 per day, respectively (see Table 2).
evidence: This is calculated from the mathematical model and shown in Table 2.

claim: In the absence of cell-to-cell infection, the Malthus coefficient is 0.49 ± 0.05 per day.
source: In the presence and absence of the cell-to-cell infection, the Malthus coefficient is calculated as 1.86 ± 0.37 and 0.49 ± 0.05 per day, respectively (see Table 2).
evidence: This is calculated from the mathematical model and shown in Table 2.

claim: Cell-to-cell infection increases the HIV-1 fitness by 3.80-fold.
source: Thus, cell-to-cell infection increases the HIV-1 fitness by 3.80-fold (corresponding to 944-fold higher viral load 5 days after the infection) and plays an important role in the rapid spread of HIV-1.
evidence: This is calculated from the Malthus coefficients with and without cell-to-cell infection.

claim: Cell-to-cell infection corresponds to 944-fold higher viral load 5 days after infection.
source: Thus, cell-to-cell infection increases the HIV-1 fitness by 3.80-fold (corresponding to 944-fold higher viral load 5 days after the infection) and plays an important role in the rapid spread of HIV-1.
evidence: This is calculated from the difference in Malthus coefficients over 5 days.

claim: The efficient viral spread via cell-to-cell infection is especially relevant at the beginning of virus infection.
source: Thus, the efficient viral spread via the cell-to-cell infection is relevant, especially at the beginning of virus infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the rapid increase in viral fitness and load.

claim: The simulated values corresponding to cell-to-cell virus propagation are closer to experimental data from coupled cell-free and cell-to-cell infection than to data from cell-free infection only.
source: In terms of the dynamics of infected cells and virus production, the simulated values corresponding to cell-to-cell virus propagation, are closer to experimental data from the coupled cell-free and cell-to-cell infection, than to data from the cell-free infection only.
evidence: This is shown in the virtual experiment results in Figure 4.

claim: The cell-free infection, which contributes approximately 40% to the whole HIV-1 infection process, plays a limited role on virus spread.
source: This shows that the cell-free infection, which contributes approximately 40% to the whole HIV-1 infection process, plays a limited role on the virus spread.
evidence: This is inferred from the virtual experiment showing cell-to-cell infection alone is nearly as effective as both modes combined.

claim: Even if cell-free infection could be completely blocked, cell-to-cell infection would still effectively spread viruses.
source: In other words, even if we could completely block the cell-free infection, the cell-to-cell infection would still effectively spread viruses (Sigal et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the modeling results and supported by citation to Sigal et al., 2011.

claim: About 60% of viral infection is attributed to cell-to-cell infection in the in vitro cell culture system.
source: Based on our calculated values of these three indexes, we found that about 60% of the viral infection is attributed to the cell-to-cell infection in the in vitro cell culture system (Table 1), which is consistent with previous estimation by Komarova and Wodarz (2013), Komarova et al. (2013a), and Komarova et al. (2013b).
evidence: This is calculated from the basic reproduction numbers and shown in Table 1.

claim: Cell-to-cell infection effectively promotes virus infection by reducing the generation time (×0.9 times).
source: In addition, we revealed that the cell-to-cell infection effectively promotes the virus infection by reducing the generation time (×0.9 times), and by increasing the Malthus coefficient (×3.80 times) (Table 2).
evidence: This is calculated from the mathematical model and shown in Table 2.

claim: Cell-to-cell infection effectively promotes virus infection by increasing the Malthus coefficient (×3.80 times).
source: In addition, we revealed that the cell-to-cell infection effectively promotes the virus infection by reducing the generation time (×0.9 times), and by increasing the Malthus coefficient (×3.80 times) (Table 2).
evidence: This is calculated from the mathematical model and shown in Table 2.

claim: The environment of immune cells in vivo is radically different from the conditions of in vitro cell cultures.
source: When we consider the significance of the cell-to-cell infection in patients infected with HIV-1, it should be noted that the environment of immune cells including CD4+ T-cells in vivo is radically different from the conditions of in vitro cell cultures.
evidence: This is stated as general biological knowledge.

claim: Lymphocytes are closely packed in lymphoid tissues such as lymph nodes.
source: For instance, lymphocytes are closely packed in lymphoid tissues such as lymph nodes, and thereby, the frequency for the infected cell to contact with adjacent uninfected cells in vivo would be much higher than that in in vitro cell cultures.
evidence: This is stated as biological knowledge about lymphoid tissue structure.

claim: The frequency for infected cells to contact adjacent uninfected cells in vivo would be much higher than in vitro.
source: For instance, lymphocytes are closely packed in lymphoid tissues such as lymph nodes, and thereby, the frequency for the infected cell to contact with adjacent uninfected cells in vivo would be much higher than that in in vitro cell cultures.
evidence: This is inferred from the knowledge that lymphocytes are closely packed in vivo.

claim: HIV-1-infected cells converge to lymph nodes and can be vehicles for viral dissemination in vivo.
source: In addition, Murooka et al. have directly demonstrated that HIV-1-infected cells converge to lymph nodes and can be vehicles for viral dissemination in vivo (Murooka et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Murooka et al., 2012.

claim: Cell-to-cell viral spread is resistant to anti-viral immunity such as neutralizing antibodies and cytotoxic T lymphocytes.
source: Moreover, certain studies have suggested that cell-to-cell viral spread is resistant to anti-viral immunity such as neutralizing antibodies and cytotoxic T lymphocytes (Martin and Sattentau, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martin and Sattentau, 2009.

claim: The contribution of cell-to-cell infection for viral propagation in vivo may be much higher than that estimated from in vitro cell culture system.
source: Therefore, these notions strongly suggest that the contribution of the cell-to-cell infection for viral propagation in vivo may be much higher than that estimated from the in vitro cell culture system.
evidence: This is inferred from the differences between in vivo and in vitro conditions.

claim: Cell-to-cell infection permits viral replication even under anti-retroviral therapy.
source: As another significance of cell-to-cell viral spread, Sigal et al. have suggested that the cell-to-cell infection permits viral replication even under the anti-retroviral therapy (Sigal et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sigal et al., 2011.

claim: The multiplicity of infection per cell in cell-to-cell infection is tremendously higher than that reached by an infectious viral particle.
source: This is attributed to the fact that the multiplicity of infection per cell is tremendously higher than that reached by an infectious viral particle.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for why cell-to-cell infection can overcome antiviral therapy.

claim: A complete block of cell-free infection provides only a limited impact on the whole HIV-1 infection.
source: Furthermore, our virtual experiments showed that a complete block of the cell-free infection, which is highly susceptible to current antiviral drugs, provides only a limited impact on the whole HIV-1 infection (Figure 3).
evidence: This is shown in the virtual experiment results in Figure 3.

claim: Cell-free infection is highly susceptible to current antiviral drugs.
source: Furthermore, our virtual experiments showed that a complete block of the cell-free infection, which is highly susceptible to current antiviral drugs, provides only a limited impact on the whole HIV-1 infection (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about antiviral drug action.

claim: Cell-to-cell infection can be a barrier to prevent the cure of HIV-1 infection.
source: Taken together, our findings further support that the cell-to-cell infection can be a barrier to prevent the cure of HIV-1 infection, which is discussed in Sigal et al. (2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the findings and supported by citation to Sigal et al., 2011.

claim: Some papers have shown that cell-to-cell spread cannot overcome the action of most anti-HIV-1 drugs.
source: However, it should be noted that some papers have shown that cell-to-cell spread cannot overcome the action of most anti-HIV-1 drugs (Titanji et al., 2013; Agosto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Titanji et al., 2013 and Agosto et al., 2014.

claim: Other viruses such as herpes simplex virus, measles virus, and human hepatitis C virus drive their dissemination via cell-to-cell infection.
source: In addition to HIV-1, other viruses such as herpes simplex virus, measles virus, and human hepatitis C virus drive their dissemination via cell-to-cell infection (Sattentau, 2008; Talbert-Slagle et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sattentau, 2008 and Talbert-Slagle et al., 2014.

claim: It was difficult to explore the impact of cell-to-cell viral spread by conventional virological experiments because an infected cell is simultaneously capable of achieving cell-to-cell infection along with producing infectious viral particles.
source: Although the impact of cell-to-cell viral spread is a topic of broad interest in virology, it was difficult to explore this issue by conventional virological experiments, because an infected cell is simultaneously capable of achieving cell-to-cell infection along with producing infectious viral particles.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of conventional experimental approaches.

claim: The synergistic strategy of experiments with mathematical modeling is a powerful approach to quantitatively elucidate the dynamics of virus infection.
source: The synergistic strategy of experiments with mathematical modeling is a powerful approach to quantitatively elucidate the dynamics of virus infection in a way that is inaccessible through conventional experimental approaches.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the success of the current study's approach.

claim: Jurkat cell line is an HIV-1-susceptible human CD4+ T-cell line.
source: Jurkat cell line (Watanabe et al., 2012) was cultured in the culture medium: RPMI 1640 (Sigma, St. Louis, MO) containing 2% fetal calf serum and antibiotics.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the cell line used, supported by citation.

claim: The virus solution was prepared from pNL4-3 plasmid transfected into 293T cells.
source: The virus solution was prepared as previously described (Sato et al., 2010, 2013, 2014; Iwami et al., 2012a). Briefly, 30 μg of pNL4-3 plasmid (Adachi et al., 1986) (GenBank accession no. M19921.2) was transfected into 293T cells by the calcium-phosphate method.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method, supported by citations.

claim: Jurkat cells were infected with HIV-1 at multiplicity of infection 0.1.
source: For HIV-1 infection, 3 × 105 of Jurkat cells were infected with HIV-1 (multiplicity of infection 0.1) at 37°C for 2 hr.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol.

claim: For the shaking infection, the infected cell culture was kept on a rocker placed in 37°C/5% CO2 incubator and gently shaken at 40 movements per min.
source: For the shaking infection, the infected cell culture was handled as previously described (Sourisseau et al., 2007). Briefly, the cell culture was kept on a Petit rocker Model-2230 (Wakenyaku, Japan) placed in 37°C/5% CO2 incubator, and was gently shaken at 40 movements per min.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol, supported by citation.

claim: The amount of virus particles in culture supernatant was quantified using an HIV-1 p24 antigen ELISA kit.
source: The amount of virus particles in the culture supernatant and the number of infected cells were routinely measured as follows: a portion (300 μl) of the infected cell culture was routinely harvested, and the amount of released virions in the culture supernatant was quantified by using an HIV-1 p24 antigen ELISA kit (ZetptoMetrix) according to the manufacture's procedure.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: The percentage of infected cells was measured by flow cytometry.
source: The percentage of infected cells was measured by flow cytometry. Flow cytometry was performed with a FACSCalibur (BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA) as previously described (Sato et al., 2010; Sato et al., 2011, 2013, 2014; Iwami et al., 2012a), and the obtained data were analyzed with CellQuest software (BD Biosciences).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method, supported by citations.

claim: The detection threshold for cell number is 3000 cells/ml.
source: The detection threshold of each value are the followings: cell number (cell counting), 3000 cells/ml; % p24-positive cells (flow cytometry), 0.3%; and p24 antigen in culture supernatant (p24 antigen ELISA), 80 pg/ml.
evidence: This is stated as a technical specification of the assay.

claim: The detection threshold for % p24-positive cells is 0.3%.
source: The detection threshold of each value are the followings: cell number (cell counting), 3000 cells/ml; % p24-positive cells (flow cytometry), 0.3%; and p24 antigen in culture supernatant (p24 antigen ELISA), 80 pg/ml.
evidence: This is stated as a technical specification of the assay.

claim: The detection threshold for p24 antigen in culture supernatant is 80 pg/ml.
source: The detection threshold of each value are the followings: cell number (cell counting), 3000 cells/ml; % p24-positive cells (flow cytometry), 0.3%; and p24 antigen in culture supernatant (p24 antigen ELISA), 80 pg/ml.
evidence: This is stated as a technical specification of the assay.

claim: The growth rate g was estimated to be 0.47 ± 0.10 per day for static culture.
source: Here we note that g and Tmax were separately estimated and fixed to be 0.47 ± 0.10 for the static culture and 0.54 ± 0.09 for the shaking culture per day, and (1.51 ± 0.02) × 106 and (1.22 ± 0.02) × 106 cells per flask of medium from the cell growth experiments, respectively (see 'Materials and methods', Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is estimated from cell growth experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The growth rate g was estimated to be 0.54 ± 0.09 per day for shaking culture.
source: Here we note that g and Tmax were separately estimated and fixed to be 0.47 ± 0.10 for the static culture and 0.54 ± 0.09 for the shaking culture per day, and (1.51 ± 0.02) × 106 and (1.22 ± 0.02) × 106 cells per flask of medium from the cell growth experiments, respectively (see 'Materials and methods', Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is estimated from cell growth experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The carrying capacity Tmax was estimated to be (1.51 ± 0.02) × 10^6 cells per flask for static culture.
source: Here we note that g and Tmax were separately estimated and fixed to be 0.47 ± 0.10 for the static culture and 0.54 ± 0.09 for the shaking culture per day, and (1.51 ± 0.02) × 106 and (1.22 ± 0.02) × 106 cells per flask of medium from the cell growth experiments, respectively (see 'Materials and methods', Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is estimated from cell growth experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The carrying capacity Tmax was estimated to be (1.22 ± 0.02) × 10^6 cells per flask for shaking culture.
source: Here we note that g and Tmax were separately estimated and fixed to be 0.47 ± 0.10 for the static culture and 0.54 ± 0.09 for the shaking culture per day, and (1.51 ± 0.02) × 106 and (1.22 ± 0.02) × 106 cells per flask of medium from the cell growth experiments, respectively (see 'Materials and methods', Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is estimated from cell growth experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The clearance rate c was set to 2.3 per day based on daily harvesting of viruses.
source: In addition, we used c value of 2.3 per day, which is estimated from daily harvesting of viruses (i.e., the amount of p24 have to be reduced by around 90% per day by the daily medium-replacement procedure).
evidence: This is estimated from the experimental protocol of daily medium replacement.

claim: The basic reproduction number R0 is defined as the number of secondly infected cells produced from a typical infected cell during its infectious period.
source: The basic reproduction number, R0, is defined as the number of the secondly infected cells produced from a typical infected cell during its infectious period.
evidence: This is the standard definition of R0 in epidemiology, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The rate constant for cell-free infection (β) averaged 4.18 ± 1.41 × 10^-6 (p24 day)^-1 across three experiments.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 as the average across three experiments.

claim: The rate constant for cell-to-cell infection (ω) averaged 1.09 ± 0.33 × 10^-6 (cell day)^-1 across three experiments.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 as the average across three experiments.

claim: The production rate of total viral protein (p) averaged 0.50 ± 0.16 day^-1 across three experiments.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 as the average across three experiments.

claim: The death rate of infected cells (δ) averaged 0.50 ± 0.10 day^-1 across three experiments.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 as the average across three experiments.
